newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bundesbank officials warn against EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bundesbank officials warn against EMU delay.

text.p: The European Union must launch its planned single currency on time or risk serious setbacks, even though Germany -- the driving force behind integration -- might itself miss key entry targets, senior German central bank officials said.

Three members of the Bundesbank's ruling council, speaking at separate events on Monday, said countries struggling to meet the fiscal criteria while recovering from severe recession should avoid any temptation to postpone the 1999 start of economic and monetary union (EMU).
On Tuesday a fourth central banker, Franz-Christoph Zeitler, said the planned currency union would be the key for economic growth.
But Zeitler, president of the state central bank in Bavaria, steered clear of the raging debate on postponing the launch.

Although delaying the start might seem like a less painful and therefore desirable option, Guntram Palm, president of the state central bank in Baden-Wuerttemberg, said talk of postponement was "totally misplaced".
Such a decision would lead to an immediate and big jump in the value of the mark, which would hurt German exports as well as stunt countries' efforts to achieve a further consolidation of finances.
One reason that talk of a delay has reached new heights is that so many nations, including Germany, appear to be at risk of missing the key criteria.
These call for budget deficits of aspiring nations to remain below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and for debts not to exceed 60 percent of GDP.

Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, president of the state central bank in Berlin and Brandenburg, said he doubted whether the German government would reach its goal of holding its budget deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997.
But three of the bank officials said that the deficit goal was only one of a number of entry criteria and that it might not be the most critical in creating a stable currency union in the long term.

The European Union's Maastricht Treaty also says that participating countries must have stable foreign exchange rates as well as low long-term interest and inflation rates. Many nations already fulfil these goals.

"In my opinion European currency union can start in January 1999 while conforming to those EMU convergence criteria that are most often discussed," said Ernst Welteke, president of the state central bank in Hesse.
Welteke said he wondered how a budget deficit of just under three percent would be good for stability while a budget deficit of slightly over three percent would be negative.
At the same time he added: "Fiscal stability in currency union is naturally a very important asset as it ensures that fiscal solidity of the individual members can be closely monitored."

Zeitler added that participating countries held the key to a monetary union's benefits, adding that advantages would improve considerably as nations stuck to the stability and credibility criteria listed in the Maastricht Treaty.

Fearing strict entry criteria could give way to creative book-keeping, Palm said: "A trick-free deficit of just over three percent in 1997 that will be further reduced in following years due to savings efforts is preferable to 2.9 percent reached through creative accounting."
Welteke added that "the three percent deficit criteria should not be a knock-out criterion", prohibiting any nation just over that level from entering.
Both Palm and Welteke believed that currency union would go ahead as planned with Germany and France since union without them would make little sense.
